lessonTitle: Crystal Structures, Packing and Miller Indices

blocks.text: A steel bar heated through 912 degrees C suddenly shrinks in length, even though the temperature is rising. The iron atoms have not changed, but they have rearranged from a BCC to a denser FCC packing.

blocks.markdown: A crystal is described by a small repeating **unit cell**. The corners of the cell are lattice points and the atoms in the cell sit on them in a pattern fixed by the structure. Most engineering metals adopt one of three: face-centred cubic (FCC), body-centred cubic (BCC) or hexagonal close-packed (HCP). Here we treat the cubic cases and model atoms as hard spheres of radius $R$ that touch along a line, which fixes the lattice parameter $a$ (the cube edge) in terms of $R$.

blocks.title: Atomic packing factor (APF)
blocks.text: The fraction of the unit-cell volume occupied by atoms, treated as hard spheres: $\mathrm{APF}=\dfrac{n\,\tfrac43\pi R^3}{a^3}$, where $n$ is the number of atoms belonging to the cell, $R$ is the atomic radius and $a$ is the lattice parameter. APF is dimensionless.

blocks.latex: n_{SC}=1,\ a=2R;\qquad n_{BCC}=2,\ a=\frac{4R}{\sqrt3};\qquad n_{FCC}=4,\ a=2\sqrt2\,R
blocks.caption: Touching direction: cube edge (SC), body diagonal (BCC), face diagonal (FCC). Atoms per cell count corner atoms as 1/8 and face atoms as 1/2.

blocks.title: APF of FCC
blocks.prompt: Calculate the atomic packing factor of the FCC structure.

steps.text: Atoms touch along the face diagonal, which has length $\sqrt2\,a$ and spans $4R$ (corner atom radius, face atom diameter, corner atom radius).
Count atoms: 8 corners at 1/8 each plus 6 faces at 1/2 each.
Atom volume per cell is $4\cdot\frac43\pi R^3=\frac{16}{3}\pi R^3$, and the cell volume is $a^3=16\sqrt2\,R^3$.

blocks.answer: APF$_{FCC}=0.74$. The same method gives $\pi/6=0.52$ for SC and $\sqrt3\pi/8=0.68$ for BCC.

blocks.caption: Cubic metal structures treated as hard spheres. HCP, with ideal $c/a$, also has coordination number 12 and APF 0.74.

blocks.markdown: **Density from the lattice.** Knowing the number of atoms per cell, $n$, the molar mass $A$ in g/mol, the cell volume $V_c=a^3$ and Avogadro's number $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$ atoms per mole, the theoretical density is the mass in the cell divided by its volume. Real metals are slightly less dense because of vacancies, grain boundaries and impurities.

blocks.caption: With $A$ in g/mol and $V_c$ in cm$^3$, $\rho$ is in g/cm$^3$; multiply by 1000 for kg/m$^3$.

blocks.title: Theoretical density of copper
blocks.prompt: Copper is FCC with atomic radius $R=0.128$ nm and $A=63.55$ g/mol. Estimate its density.
blocks.answer: $\rho\approx8.90$ g/cm$^3$ ($8.90\times10^3$ kg/m$^3$); the typical measured value is about 8.9 to 8.96 g/cm$^3$, so the model is good.

blocks.markdown:
**Directions and planes.** Cubic indices are found by simple rules, using axes $x$, $y$, $z$ along the cube edges in units of $a$.

- *Direction $[uvw]$*: subtract the tail coordinates from the head coordinates, clear fractions by multiplying by the smallest common factor, and write negatives with a bar, e.g. $[\bar{1}10]$.
- *Plane $(hkl)$*: take the intercepts with the axes (move the origin if the plane passes through it), invert them, and clear fractions. A plane parallel to an axis has an infinite intercept and index 0.
- In cubic crystals only, the direction $[hkl]$ is perpendicular to the plane $(hkl)$.
- Families are written $\langle uvw\rangle$ and $\{hkl\}$ and contain all equivalent directions and planes.

items: FCC: closest-packed planes are $\{111\}$ and closest-packed directions are $\langle110\rangle$.
BCC: closest-packed directions are $\langle111\rangle$; there are no truly close-packed planes.
The stacking of close-packed planes explains why FCC and HCP, both with APF 0.74, are different structures.
Indices depend only on ratios, so $(220)$ is the same orientation as $(110)$ and is reduced.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: Indices are reciprocals of intercepts, not the intercepts themselves, and a direction needs head minus tail. Do not count shared atoms as whole atoms: corner atoms count 1/8 and face atoms 1/2.

points: APF is atoms per cell times atomic volume divided by cell volume: 0.52 (SC), 0.68 (BCC), 0.74 (FCC).
Theoretical density is $\rho = nA/(V_c N_A)$, with $n$ = 4 for FCC, 2 for BCC.
Plane indices come from reciprocal intercepts; direction indices from head minus tail; in cubic crystals $[hkl]\perp(hkl)$.

questions.stem: How many atoms belong entirely to one conventional BCC unit cell?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 8 corner atoms each shared by 8 cells (8 x 1/8 = 1) plus 1 atom at the body centre.
distractorRationale.b: This is the count for simple cubic, where only the corner atoms exist.
distractorRationale.c: This is the FCC count (8 x 1/8 + 6 x 1/2); BCC has no face-centre atoms.
distractorRationale.d: This counts all the atom positions without allowing for sharing between neighbouring cells.

questions.explanation: Atoms on cell corners are shared by eight cells and contribute 1/8 each, so eight corners give one atom, and the body-centre atom belongs wholly to the cell. The total is $8\times\frac18+1=2$ atoms per BCC cell.

questions.stem: Which crystal structure has a coordination number of 12 and an atomic packing factor of about 0.74 for hard spheres of one size?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: each atom touches 12 neighbours and the packing factor is $\pi/(3\sqrt2)=0.74$.
distractorRationale.b: BCC has 8 touching neighbours and APF 0.68.
distractorRationale.d: Diamond cubic has only 4 neighbours and a very low APF of about 0.34.

questions.explanation: In FCC the atoms touch along the face diagonal and each atom has 12 nearest neighbours; the packing factor is the maximum possible for equal spheres. BCC (8 neighbours, 0.68) and SC (6 neighbours, 0.52) are less dense.

questions.stem: A simple cubic unit cell has a higher atomic packing factor than a BCC unit cell.
questions.explanation: The simple cubic APF is $\pi/6\approx0.52$, whereas BCC is $\sqrt3\pi/8\approx0.68$. BCC packs better because the body-centre atom fills part of the large gap at the centre of the cube.

questions.stem: Tungsten has a BCC structure with a lattice parameter $a = 0.3165$ nm and an atomic mass $A = 183.84$ g/mol. Using Avogadro's number $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$, calculate the theoretical density in g/cm$^3$.
questions.explanation: BCC has $n=2$ atoms per cell, so $\rho=nA/(V_cN_A)$ with $V_c=a^3=(0.3165\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm})^3=3.171\times10^{-23}$ cm$^3$. Then $\rho=2(183.84)/(3.171\times10^{-23}\times6.022\times10^{23})=19.26$ g/cm$^3$.

questions.stem: Iron in its BCC form can be modelled as hard spheres of atomic radius $R = 0.1241$ nm that touch along the cube body diagonal. Calculate the lattice parameter $a$ in nm.
questions.explanation: In BCC the atoms touch along the body diagonal of length $\sqrt3\,a$, and that diagonal spans $4R$ (a corner atom, the centre atom and a corner atom: $R+2R+R$). Hence $a=4R/\sqrt3=4(0.1241)/1.7321=0.2866$ nm.

questions.stem: A plane in a cubic crystal cuts the $x$ axis at $a/2$, the $y$ axis at $a$ and is parallel to the $z$ axis. What are its Miller indices?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: intercepts in units of $a$ are 1/2, 1, infinity; reciprocals 2, 1, 0.
distractorRationale.b: The reciprocals have been assigned to the wrong axes.
distractorRationale.c: Miller indices are reciprocals of intercepts, reduced to integers; the intercepts themselves are not the indices.
distractorRationale.d: A plane parallel to $z$ has an infinite intercept, giving index 0, not 1.

questions.explanation: Take the intercepts in units of the lattice parameter (1/2, 1, infinity), invert them to get (2, 1, 0), and clear fractions if any remain. The infinite intercept gives index zero because the plane never meets the $z$ axis.

questions.stem: A direction in a cubic crystal runs from the point $(\tfrac12,0,0)$ to the point $(0,1,1)$, in units of the lattice parameter. What are its indices?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: head minus tail is $(-\tfrac12,1,1)$; multiplying by 2 gives $(-1,2,2)$.
distractorRationale.b: This is just the tail position, not the head minus the tail.
distractorRationale.c: The sign of the first component has been dropped; $-\tfrac12$ becomes $\bar 1$, not 1.
distractorRationale.d: This is the head coordinates alone; the tail must be subtracted.

questions.explanation: A direction is found by subtracting the tail coordinates from the head coordinates, giving $(-\tfrac12,1,1)$, then multiplying by the smallest factor that clears fractions (here 2). Negative components are written with a bar over the integer.

questions.stem: An element is available as FCC with hard-sphere atoms of radius $R$ or, hypothetically, as BCC with the same $R$ and the same atomic mass. How do the two theoretical densities compare?

options.text: The FCC density is about 9 percent higher
The densities are identical because the atoms are identical
The BCC density is about 9 percent higher
The FCC density is twice the BCC density

questions.correctOptionText: The FCC density is about 9 percent higher

distractorRationale.b: Same atoms does not mean same density: the FCC arrangement packs more atoms into a given volume.
distractorRationale.c: Reversed: BCC has fewer atoms per unit volume of crystal.
distractorRationale.d: FCC has twice as many atoms per cell, but its cell is also larger, so the ratio is far smaller than 2.

questions.explanation: Density scales with atoms per cell divided by cell volume. FCC: $4/(2\sqrt2R)^3$; BCC: $2/(4R/\sqrt3)^3$. The ratio of these is 1.089, which is equivalent to the ratio of the packing factors, $0.7405/0.6802=1.089$.

questions.stem: Derive the atomic packing factor of the BCC structure, stating the geometric relation between the atomic radius $R$ and the lattice parameter $a$, and the number of atoms per cell.
markingGuide: Atoms touch along the body diagonal, which has length $\sqrt3 a = 4R$ (2 marks)
Two atoms per cell (corner 8 x 1/8 plus 1 centre) (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The packing factor is the volume of atoms in a cell divided by the cell volume. With $a=4R/\sqrt3$, $a^3=64R^3/(3\sqrt3)$, so $\mathrm{APF}=\frac{8\pi R^3/3}{64R^3/(3\sqrt3)}=\frac{\sqrt3\pi}{8}=0.680$.

questions.stem: In a cubic crystal, the plane $(hkl)$ and the direction $[hkl]$ are perpendicular. Verify this for the plane with intercepts $a$, $a$ and $a$ (the $(111)$ plane) and the direction $[111]$, and then state the Miller indices of the plane with intercepts $a/3$, $a/2$ and $\infty$.
markingGuide: For the (111) plane, the in-plane vectors can be taken as $(-1,1,0)$ and $(-1,0,1)$ (1 mark)
Dot products with $[111]$: $(-1+1+0)=0$ and $(-1+0+1)=0$, so [111] is normal to the plane (2 marks)
Reciprocals of the intercepts $1/3, 1/2, \infty$ are 3, 2, 0 (1 mark)
Note that no common factor can be removed from (320) (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Two in-plane vectors can be formed from the three intercept points, and the direction [111] has zero dot product with both, so it is normal to the plane. The reciprocals of the intercepts $1/3$, $1/2$ and $\infty$ are 3, 2 and 0, giving $(320)$.
